title: Hash-based indexing
lead: Static hashing, collisions, extendible hashing and directory growth.

sections.title: Hashing and equality lookup
sections.html:
Hashing semantics and collision strategies

A hash table implements a key→value association. Chaining stores collisions in a linked structure; open addressing probes alternative slots in one array (linear, cuckoo and Robin Hood are source examples). Disk indexing instead groups entries in bucket pages so page-I/O behaviour dominates.

Equal keys always choose the same bucket; unequal keys can collide. This supports equality lookup, duplicate elimination, grouping and equality joins. Hash order does not preserve inequalities, so it cannot locate an arbitrary range without inspecting unrelated buckets. Static chained hashing fixes the bucket set; extendible hashing grows it. Linear hashing is named but not developed in these slides.

PDF pp. 1–6

sections.title: Static chained hashing
sections.html:
Static bucket operations

Allocate N primary pages and define h(key) in 0…N−1. To search, compute h(k), read that bucket and compare actual keys through its overflow chain. For a unique key, finding it permits termination; for nonunique keys, collect every match.

Insert into a free bucket position or allocate an overflow page; delete the matching entry and update storage as required. Without overflow, the source estimates one read for lookup and read+write for modification. Fetching the heap record is additional for by-reference entries. Long chains add reads and make per-key performance uneven.

PDF pp. 7–10

Hash distribution and resizing cost

h(k)=k mod N maps to the required range, but regular key patterns can collide badly. With N=2ᵈ, only d low bits determine the bucket; prime moduli can avoid some periodic patterns, but distribution still depends on data and the hash function. The source lists lightweight noncryptographic alternatives.

Growth creates overflow; shrinkage wastes primary pages. Rehashing reads and rebuilds the entire index to restore room, potentially interrupting access in the simple scheme. Static buckets have a concurrency advantage: many updates affect only one chain rather than a global routing structure.

PDF pp. 11–12

sections.title: Extendible hashing and depth
sections.html:
Directory, global depth and local depth

Extendible hashing adds a pointer directory. Global depth g gives 2ᵍ directory slots indexed by low hash bits in this source. A bucket with local depth d is selected by 2ᵍ⁻ᵈ slots; its entries share the last d bits.

The source starts g=2: slots 00 and 10 share an even bucket with local depth 1 and hash values 8,14; slot 01 points to [21,25] at depth 2; slot 11 points to [11] at depth 2. The displayed values are h(key), not necessarily the actual search keys.

PDF pp. 13–15

Lookup A and insertion B

For h(A)=14=01110₂, low bits 10 choose the even bucket. Compare A’s actual key against bucket entries, since equal hashes are not proof of equal keys.

For h(B)=29=11101₂, low bits 01 select [21,25]. The source bucket has capacity three, so inserting B makes [21,25,29] without changing depth or directory pointers. The old even and 11 buckets are unaffected.

PDF pp. 16–20

sections.title: Bucket splits and directory doubling
sections.html:
Insertion C and the complete split

h(C)=5=00101; low2=01 -> full [21,25,29]
split using low3 bits:
  25=11001 -> 001 bucket, localDepth3
  21=10101,29=11101 -> 101 bucket, localDepth3
localDepth3 exceeds globalDepth2 -> double directory to g=3
insert5 into 101 -> [21,29,5]
even bucket [8,14] is still shared by 000,010,100,110
[11] is still shared by 011,111

Only the overflowing bucket’s entries are redistributed. Doubling copies pointers, not every data entry. A key collision unresolved by another bit can require further splitting; an implementation must handle extreme equal-hash cases explicitly.

PDF pp. 21–24

When doubling is unnecessary

If local depth d<g, a split uses the extra bit already represented by the directory. Increase local depth and redirect the relevant half of its pointers; global depth remains unchanged. Doubling is needed only when the split bucket had d=g.

Buckets may be merged with compatible buddies after deletions, and a directory can shrink when its pointer structure permits. These conditions follow from shared-prefix/suffix routing, not simply from total entry count. Static hashing trades chains against wasted space; extendible hashing trades targeted splits against directory overhead.

PDF pp. 25–26

quiz.question: A bucket with local depth 2 and global depth 4 is split into buckets with local depth 3. Which statement is correct?
options: The directory does not need to double
quiz.explanation: Before the split the directory uses four bits. The split only needs three bits to distinguish the two new buckets, so the existing directory is already sufficient. The old bucket has 2^(4−2)=4 pointers; after redirection each new depth-three bucket has 2^(4−3)=2. Other buckets need not split.
